newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK resists scandal probe, issues spy denial.
newsitem.headline: HK resists scandal probe, issues spy denial.

text.p: Hong Kong's top civil servant on Wednesday denied that a former immigration chief was a spy, but the government blocked attempts by an inquiry panel to see security reports on the disgraced official.
Chief Secretary Anson Chan, testifying under oath to a Legislative Council select committee, slapped down suggestions that Immigration Director Laurence Leung was a spy for China.
"There is no evidence and no reason to suppose that Mr Leung is or was a Chinese agent," Chan told the panel.
Her statement was the government's clearest denial so far that Leung had spied. But the administration refused to release vetting and anti-graft reports on 55-year-old Leung.

Leung's post was highly sensitive because he had authority over immigration, nationality and frontier affairs, as well as access to confidential information on citizens, which carries security implications ahead of Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on July 1.

Some panellists were sceptical that the government's reasons for forcing Leung to retire -- that he concealed his business dealings and violated repayment terms on a government loan -- were enough to justify his removal last July.
The government originally said Leung had quit for personal reasons but then last week accused him of lapses in integrity.
Chan said there was no evidence that Leung gave China details of Hong Kong residents seeking British passports under a special scheme, or on Chinese asylum-seekers in Hong Kong.

"There is no evidence and no reason to believe that the list of (passport) beneficiaries has been compromised. In any case, Mr Leung, as Director of Immigration, did not personally hold such a list," she said.

"There is no evidence he has passed on information on asylum-seekers to an unauthorised party. He did not hold such information, and there's no record of his seeking to acquire it," said Chan, second in seniority to colonial Governor Chris Patten.
Chan and government personnel boss Lam Woon-kwong told the panel the security reports, which included a videotape of police questioning Leung, were confidential.
But Chan showed the panel a letter from Hong Kong's anti-corruption body and offered it the opportunity to view a videotape on the affair before its next sitting.
The panel agreed to hold most of Wednesday's session behind closed doors after Lam and Chan asked for this. Earlier sessions of the probe have been open to the press.

The two officials said disclosing the full reports could undermine anti-graft operations and the personnel vetting system, making it impossible for the government to carry out effective checks on its staff in the future.
The reports -- one by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) and one by the police -- were cited earlier by Lam as the basis for removing Leung.
Panel chairman Ip Kwok-him told reporters after the hearing he was shocked after looking at the anti-graft fighters' report. But he gave no details.
During the open part of the session, Chan hedged when asked by a panellist whether Leung's dismissal was related to arms trade links with a mainland China company.
"We are not aware of (this business link)," Chan said.
